abstract: Ribosomopathies are a class of disorders caused by defects in the structure or function of the ribosome and are characterized by tissue-specific abnormalities. Diamond Blackfan anemia syndrome (DBAS) features skeletal anomalies in addition to anemia, but whether these reflect primary mesenchymal dysfunction remains unknown. Here, we demonstrate that skeletal growth retardation in DBAS is cell-autonomous, arising from RPS19 haploinsufficiency in mesenchymal progenitors without leading to hematopoietic failure. RPS19 haploinsufficient mice exhibit shorter limbs due to growth plate disorganization. Single-cell RNA sequencing reveals impaired chondrocyte differentiation, with decreased Runx2 expression and activation of the p53 pathway across the chondrocyte trajectory. Surprisingly, in vivo translation remains unchanged, arguing against a translational collapse and implying the p53-dependent nucleolar surveillance as main mechanism of growth defect. Accordingly, Trp53 deletion in RPS19 haploinsufficient mice rescues all skeletal defects in a dose-dependent manner. Importantly, RPL5 haploinsufficiency in mesenchymal progenitors does not result in skeletal defects, establishing ribosomal protein gene specific functions in the mesenchyme. These findings demonstrate that nucleolar surveillance functions as a developmental checkpoint controlling growth plate formation, with direct implications for understanding the tissue-specific manifestations of ribosomopathies.
